title: The heavens declare
hook: the heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was mysterium tremendum: awe, terrible and fascinating at once. Your line was look up.

No words, and yet a voice that reaches everywhere. That's the puzzle at the center of a short psalm, the nineteenth in the Bible's book of Psalms. Its writer looks up, and what comes out isn't a description of the sky. It's a claim that the sky is talking: not in Hebrew, not in any language, and never silent. It belongs to the Jewish and Christian scriptures, and some readers from other homes keep its first line for their own looking. On the thousandth day of this path, here it is.
screen: `NO WORDS, YET A VOICE.` → `THE SKY IS TALKING.` → `PSALM 19.`

segments.voice: First, the opening line, in the King James words: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." Declare is a strong verb. The sky isn't just pretty; it's telling something, the way a messenger tells news. Second, the rhythm: "Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge." Each day hands the message to the next, each night to the next night, like a relay that has never stopped. You didn't miss the start; it's still going. Third, the riddle. The King James reads: "There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard." Some readers hear the Hebrew differently: there is no speech, there are no words, their voice is not heard. And yet, the next verse says, it goes out through all the earth. A speech made of no words at all. Maybe that's why it reaches everyone: nobody needs a translation. Fourth, the turn. Halfway through, the psalm moves from the sky to the teaching: "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul". The same writer reads two books, the heavens above and the words in hand, and finds them saying something alike. For someone on this path, of any faith or none, the first book is open every evening. You don't have to agree with what it says to stand still and listen.
screen: `THE SKY IS TELLING SOMETHING.` · `DAY UNTO DAY, NIGHT UNTO NIGHT.` · `A SPEECH WITH NO WORDS.` · `TWO BOOKS: SKY AND TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE HEAVENS DECLARE.`

segments.voice: Look at the sky now, through a window or outside, whatever's there: the blue or the gray, a star, a plane, the town's glow on the clouds. Listen with your eyes, the way you'd listen to someone speaking a language you don't know: not the words, the tone. If you pray, you can say the psalm's first line quietly and leave the rest to the sky.
Firmament. The sky itself, which the psalm says shows God's handiwork and speaks, day to day and night to night, with no words. Today's word.
Your line: day unto day uttereth speech. The relay has been running the whole time, every evening and every dawn. That's day one thousand.

howItsDone: Psalm 19 is prayed in Jewish and Christian worship; some people on other paths read its first line outdoors, at sunrise or under the night sky.

chat.says: How can a psalm say the sky speaks, if it has no words?
options: Its riddle: some read it as having no words, yet its voice goes through all the earth.
It means the ancient writers heard actual voices speaking in the thunder.
